groups.title: Diffusion (parabolic)
groups.blurbHtml: Smoothing, irreversible, and stiff: an explicit step is limited by Δt≤h2/2, so the working methods are implicit and the work is a tridiagonal solve.

groups.title: Waves and transport (hyperbolic)
groups.blurbHtml: Information moves at a finite speed along characteristics. Nothing smooths the solution, so the scheme's own dissipation and dispersion are what you see, and shocks need conservation.

groups.title: Steady states and modes (elliptic)
groups.blurbHtml: No time to march through: every unknown depends on every other, and the work is a large sparse linear system or its eigenvalues.

groups.title: Waves whose speed depends on wavelength (dispersive)
groups.blurbHtml: The linear part is exact in Fourier space for any time step, so these are split-step spectral codes built on fft.

groups.title: A nonlinearity against diffusion (nonlinear parabolic)
groups.blurbHtml: Steepening or growth on one side, diffusion on the other, and a front whose width and speed are set by the balance.

solvers.title: The heat equation
solvers.equationHtml: ut​=κuxx​
solvers.methodHtml: Crank-Nicolson: implicit, second order in space and time, stable at any time step
solvers.checksHtml: the exact decay of a sine mode; the measured order of accuracy; and that the explicit scheme blows up exactly where theory says it must
notes: A rod with its ends held at zero and a half-sine of heat along it. Diffusion damps a mode sin(mπx) at the rate κ(mπ)2, so the exact solution is u(x,t)=e−κπ2tsin(πx) — one number to get right, at every point.

The obvious scheme, forward in time and centered in space, is stable only while r=κΔt/Δx2≤21​: halve the grid spacing and the time step must fall by four. Crank-Nicolson averages the space derivative between the old and new time levels. That costs a tridiagonal solve per step and buys unconditional stability and second order in time. tridiag_solve is the Thomas algorithm.

solvers.title: The heat equation in two dimensions
solvers.equationHtml: ut​=uxx​+uyy​
solvers.methodHtml: alternating-direction implicit (Peaceman-Rachford): one tridiagonal solve per grid line, per half-step
solvers.checksHtml: two decaying modes against their exact rates, the measured order, and a time step 128 times the explicit limit
notes: In two dimensions an implicit step couples every point to its four neighbors, and the matrix is no longer tridiagonal. Peaceman and Rachford's way around it: split the step in half, and be implicit in one direction at a time.

First half: implicit in y, explicit in x. Second half: the other way around. Each half is a set of independent one-dimensional problems — one tridiagonal solve per grid line — so a step costs O(N) for N unknowns, the same as an explicit step. It is still second order in time and stable for any time step, which the explicit scheme is not: that one needs Δt≤h2/4.
The second half-step is the first with the axes exchanged, so it is written as transpose, the same sweep, transpose back.

The test field is two modes with different wavenumbers in x and y, sinπxsin2πy+21​sin3πxsinπy, decaying at 5π2 and 10π2. A field symmetric in x and y would not notice the two sweeps being mixed up; this one does.
solvers.source:
pi = 3.141592653589793

#| The exact solution at time t on the padded (n+2) x (n+2) grid, boundary ring included.
def exact_field(n, t) {
    h = 1.0 / (n + 1.0)
    u = zeros(n + 2.0, n + 2.0)
    for i to n + 2.0 {
        for j to n + 2.0 {
            x = i * h
            y = j * h
            u[i, j] = exp(-5.0 * pi * pi * t) * sin(pi * x) * sin(2.0 * pi * y) + 0.5 * exp(-10.0 * pi * pi * t) * sin(3.0 * pi * x) * sin(pi * y)
        }
    }
    return u
}

#| Half a step: explicit along axis 0, implicit along axis 1. `r` is dt / h^2.
#| Every interior row is its own tridiagonal system; the boundary rows of each are the identity.
def half_step(u, r) {
    m = len(u)
    lo = zeros(m) - 0.5 * r
    di = zeros(m) + (1.0 + r)
    up = zeros(m) - 0.5 * r
    di[0] = 1.0
    up[0] = 0.0
    lo[m - 1.0] = 0.0
    di[m - 1.0] = 1.0
    rhs = u + 0.5 * r * (roll(u, 1.0, 0.0) - 2.0 * u + roll(u, -1.0, 0.0))
    out = zeros(m, m)
    for i to m - 2.0 {
        row = slab(rhs, i + 1.0)
        row[0] = 0.0
        row[m - 1.0] = 0.0
        setslab(out, i + 1.0, tridiag_solve(lo, di, up, row))
    }
    return out
}

#| One Peaceman-Rachford step.
def adi_step(u, r) {
    half = half_step(u, r)
    return transpose(half_step(transpose(half), r))
}

#| March to t_end and return the largest error against the exact field.
def adi_error(n, steps, t_end) {
    h = 1.0 / (n + 1.0)
    r = (t_end / steps) / (h * h)
    u = exact_field(n, 0.0)
    for s to steps {
        u = adi_step(u, r)
    }
    return take the largest difference between u and exact_field(n, t_end)
}

T_END = 0.02
e1 = adi_error(19.0, 10.0, T_END)
e2 = adi_error(39.0, 20.0, T_END)
order = log(e1 / e2) / log(2.0)
e3 = adi_error(79.0, 40.0, T_END)
amplitude = max(abs(exact_field(79.0, T_END)))
show e1
show e2
show e3
show order
show amplitude

# 4 steps on a 79 x 79 grid: dt / h^2 = 32, against an explicit limit of 1/4
big_r = (T_END / 4.0) * 80.0 * 80.0
big_step_error = adi_error(79.0, 4.0, T_END)
show big_r
show big_step_error

N = 39
H = 1.0 / (N + 1.0)
U = exact_field(N, 0.0)
FIG_STEPS = 20.0   # the figure's run: T_END in this many steps
for s to FIG_STEPS {
    U = adi_step(U, (T_END / FIG_STEPS) / (H * H))
}

# U[i, j] is the temperature at x = i h, y = j h: transposed, x runs across and y up;
# the field is signed, so the colors are centered on zero
figure("Two modes after t = 0.02: the faster one has nearly gone", "x", "y")
origin("lower")
colormap("diverging")
plot2d(transpose(U), "u")

test "both modes decay at their exact rates: the worst error is under a thousandth of the field" {
    assert_lt(e3, 1.0e-3 * amplitude)
}
test "halving h and the time step together cuts the error by four: second order in both" {
    assert_near(order, 2.0, 0.1)
}
test "a time step 128 times the explicit limit is still stable, and still accurate to a percent of the field" {
    assert_gt(big_r, 32.0 - 1.0e-9)
    assert_lt(big_step_error, 1.0e-2 * amplitude)
}

solvers.title: The Black-Scholes equation
solvers.equationHtml: Vt​+21​σ2S2VSS​+rSVS​−rV=0
solvers.methodHtml: Crank-Nicolson on a grid in the stock price, started with four implicit half-steps (Rannacher)
solvers.checksHtml: a European call against the closed form: the price, the delta, and the measured order with and without the start-up steps
notes: The price V(S,t) of an option on a stock at price S. It is a heat equation run backward from a known final condition — at expiry T a call is worth its payoff, max(S−K,0) — with diffusion 21​σ2S2 that grows with S, a drift, and a decay at the interest rate. Counting time to expiry, τ=T−t, turns it into an ordinary forward march.

The coefficients vary along the grid, so the tridiagonal matrix is three arrays rather than three numbers, and that is the only change from the heat equation. At S=0 the call is worthless; at the far edge it is worth S−Ke−rτ, the stock less the discounted strike.

The payoff has a kink at the strike, and Crank-Nicolson does not damp the high-frequency error a kink excites: every mode's amplification tends to −1 as Δτ/h2 grows, so the error flips sign each step and never decays. It shows up in the derivatives — the delta VS​ — at the strike. Rannacher's remedy is to take the first steps with implicit Euler, which damps those modes hard, and only then switch. Both versions are run below, and their orders measured.
solvers.sourceHtml: K = 100.0 #: K strike RATE = 0.05 #: RATE risk-free interest rate, per year SIGMA = 0.2 #: SIGMA volatility, per root-year T = 1.0 #: T time to expiry, years SMAX = 300.0 #: SMAX where the grid stops: three strikes out SMOOTHED = 2.0 #: SMOOTHED how many opening steps `smooth` replaces by two half-steps each #| The standard normal cumulative distribution. def normal_cdf(x) { return 0.5 * (1.0 + erf(x / sqrt(2.0))) } #| The Black-Scholes closed form for a European call at stock price s. def call_exact(s) { d1 = (log(s / K) + (RATE + 0.5 * SIGMA * SIGMA) * T) / (SIGMA * sqrt(T)) d2 = d1 - SIGMA * sqrt(T) return s * normal_cdf(d1) - K * exp(-RATE * T) * normal_cdf(d2) } #| Its delta, dV/dS = N(d1). def delta_exact(s) { d1 = (log(s / K) + (RATE + 0.5 * SIGMA * SIGMA) * T) / (SIGMA * sqrt(T)) return normal_cdf(d1) } #| One theta-step of length dt from time-to-expiry tau: theta = 1 is implicit Euler, #| theta = 1/2 Crank-Nicolson. `s` holds the n interior stock prices, spacing h. def theta_step(v, s, h, tau, dt, theta) { n = len(v) diff = 0.5 * SIGMA * SIGMA * s * s / (h * h) drift = 0.5 * RATE * s / h low = diff - drift mid = -2.0 * diff - RATE high = diff + drift e = (1.0 - theta) * dt rhs = v + e * (low * roll(v, 1.0) + mid * v + high * roll(v, -1.0)) # roll wraps around; the two edge rows see the boundary values instead edge_old = SMAX - K * exp(-RATE * tau) edge_new = SMAX - K * exp(-RATE * (tau + dt)) last = n - 1.0 rhs[0] = v[0] + e * (mid[0] * v[0] + high[0] * v[1]) rhs[last] = v[last] + e * (low[last] * v[last - 1.0] + mid[last] * v[last] + high[last] * edge_old) + theta * dt * high[last] * edge_new return tridiag_solve(-theta * dt * low, 1.0 - theta * dt * mid, -theta * dt * high, rhs) } #| Price the call on n interior points in `steps` time steps. With `smooth`, the first two #| steps are each replaced by two implicit-Euler half-steps. def price_call(n, steps, smooth: Bool) { h = SMAX / (n + 1.0) s = linspace(h, SMAX - h, n) v = max(s - K, 0.0) dt = T / steps tau = 0.0 first = 0.0 if smooth { for q to 2.0 * SMOOTHED { v = theta_step(v, s, h, tau, 0.5 * dt, 1.0) tau = tau + 0.5 * dt } first = SMOOTHED } for m to steps - first { v = theta_step(v, s, h, tau, dt, 0.5) tau = tau + dt } return v } #| The worst error in the delta (a centered difference of the prices) within 20 of the strike. def delta_error(n, steps, smooth: Bool) { h = SMAX / (n + 1.0) v = price_call(n, steps, smooth) worst = 0.0 for i to n - 2.0 { s = (i + 2.0) * h if abs(s - K) < 20.0 { d = (v[i + 2.0] - v[i]) / (2.0 * h) worst = max(worst, abs(d - delta_exact(s))) } } return worst } #| The error in the at-the-money price. The strike sits on a grid point: (n + 1) / 3 is whole. def price_error(n, steps, smooth: Bool) { v = price_call(n, steps, smooth) return abs(v[(n + 1.0) / 3.0 - 1.0] - call_exact(K)) } N = 599 STEPS = 200 S = linspace(SMAX / (N + 1.0), SMAX - SMAX / (N + 1.0), N) V = price_call(N, STEPS, true) exact = call_exact(K) computed = V[(N + 1.0) / 3.0 - 1.0] show exact show computed # few, long time steps make dt / h^2 large: that is where the kink shows rough = delta_error(599.0, 25.0, false) smoothed = delta_error(599.0, 25.0, true) show rough show smoothed order = log(price_error(149.0, 50.0, true) / price_error(299.0, 100.0, true)) / log(2.0) show order figure("A European call, one year from expiry", "stock price S", "value") plot(S, max(S - K, 0.0), "payoff at expiry") plot(S, V, "value today") test "the at-the-money price matches the closed form to a tenth of a cent" { assert_near(computed, exact, 1.0e-3) } test "halving h and the time step together cuts the error by four: second order" { assert_near(order, 2.0, 0.1) } test "with long time steps, plain Crank-Nicolson leaves the kink ringing in the delta" { assert_gt(rough, 10.0 * smoothed) } test "four implicit half-steps at the start remove it" { assert_lt(smoothed, 1.0e-3) } # SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0 # SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 The Viv authors

solvers.title: The advection equation
solvers.equationHtml: ut​+cux​=0
solvers.methodHtml: upwind (first order) and Lax-Wendroff (second order), on a periodic grid
solvers.checksHtml: that one trip around the ring returns the pulse to where it started; and both measured orders
notes: The simplest wave equation: whatever shape you start with slides along at speed c, unchanged. On a ring of length 1 it is back where it began after a time 1/c, which makes the exact answer the initial condition itself.

It is also the equation that teaches humility about finite differences. Upwind takes the difference from the side the wave is coming from; it is stable for ν=cΔt/Δx≤1 and first order, and what it does to the error is diffuse it: the pulse spreads and sinks. Lax-Wendroff adds the second-order term of the Taylor series in time, 21​ν2(ui+1​−2ui​+ui−1​), and is second order: the pulse keeps its height and grows a small oscillating wake instead.
Periodic boundaries are where roll earns its place: a neighbor is a circular shift, and each scheme is one line.
solvers.sourceHtml: pi = 3.141592653589793 C = 1.0 NU = 0.5 #: NU the Courant number c dt / dx #| A smooth pulse on the ring. def pulse(x) { return exp(-100.0 * (x - 0.5) * (x - 0.5)) } #| Carry the pulse once around the ring with the upwind scheme; return what comes back. def upwind_lap(n) { x = linspace(0.0, 1.0 - 1.0 / n, n) u = pulse(x) steps = n / (C * NU) for s to steps { u = u - NU * (u - roll(u, 1.0)) } return u } #| The same trip with Lax-Wendroff. def lax_wendroff_lap(n) { x = linspace(0.0, 1.0 - 1.0 / n, n) u = pulse(x) steps = n / (C * NU) for s to steps { right = roll(u, -1.0) left = roll(u, 1.0) u = u - 0.5 * NU * (right - left) + 0.5 * NU * NU * (right - 2.0 * u + left) } return u } #| L2 distance between what came back and what set out. def lap_error(u, n) { x = linspace(0.0, 1.0 - 1.0 / n, n) d = u - pulse(x) return sqrt(sum(d * d) / n) } # upwind reaches its asymptotic order slowly, so it is measured on finer grids than it is drawn on up1 = lap_error(upwind_lap(1600.0), 1600.0) up2 = lap_error(upwind_lap(3200.0), 3200.0) up_coarse = lap_error(upwind_lap(400.0), 400.0) lw1 = lap_error(lax_wendroff_lap(200.0), 200.0) lw2 = lap_error(lax_wendroff_lap(400.0), 400.0) order_upwind = log(up1 / up2) / log(2.0) order_lw = log(lw1 / lw2) / log(2.0) show order_upwind show order_lw show up_coarse show lw2 N = 200 X = linspace(0.0, 1.0 - 1.0 / N, N) figure("One trip around the ring", "x", "u") plot(X, pulse(X), "exact (the starting pulse)") plot(X, upwind_lap(N), "upwind: it diffuses") plot(X, lax_wendroff_lap(N), "Lax-Wendroff: it keeps its height") style("exact (the starting pulse)", "dash") test "upwind is first order (measured between n = 1600 and 3200: it gets there slowly)" { assert_near(order_upwind, 1.0, 0.05) } test "Lax-Wendroff is second order" { assert_near(order_lw, 2.0, 0.15) } test "at the same resolution Lax-Wendroff is more than ten times closer" { assert_lt(lw2 * 10.0, up_coarse) } # SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0 # SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 The Viv authors

solvers.title: The wave equation
solvers.equationHtml: utt​=c2uxx​
solvers.methodHtml: leapfrog: centered in time and space, second order, explicit
solvers.checksHtml: a standing wave against its exact solution; the measured order; and that the energy does not drift
notes: A string fixed at both ends, plucked into its fundamental: u=sin(πx)cos(πct). Centered differences in both variables give the leapfrog scheme, un+1=2un−un−1+ν2(ui+1​−2ui​+ui−1​), with ν=cΔt/Δx.

Leapfrog has no dissipation at all — its amplification factor has modulus one for ν≤1 — so the string's energy, 21​∫(ut2​+c2ux2​)dx, should neither grow nor decay over many periods. That is the test a diffusive scheme cannot pass.

The first step needs care. Leapfrog wants two earlier levels and the problem gives one, plus an initial velocity; taking u1=u0+21​ν2δ2u0 (a Taylor step, with zero velocity) keeps the whole run second order. A plain copy would make it first.
solvers.source:
pi = 3.141592653589793
C = 1.0
NU = 0.8

#| The second difference of u, with both ends held at zero.
def second_difference(u, n) {
    d = -2.0 * u
    for i to n {
        if i > 0.0 { d[i] = d[i] + u[i - 1.0] }
        if i < n - 1.0 { d[i] = d[i] + u[i + 1.0] }
    }
    return d
}

#| Leapfrog to t_end on n interior points; the L2 error against sin(pi x) cos(pi c t).
def standing_wave_error(n, t_end) {
    h = 1.0 / (n + 1.0)
    steps = round(t_end * C / (NU * h))
    dt = t_end / steps
    nu = C * dt / h
    x = linspace(h, 1.0 - h, n)
    old = sin(pi * x)
    u = old + 0.5 * nu * nu * second_difference(old, n)
    for s to steps - 1.0 {
        new = 2.0 * u - old + nu * nu * second_difference(u, n)
        old = u
        u = new
    }
    d = u - sin(pi * x) * cos(pi * C * t_end)
    return sqrt(sum(d * d) * h)
}

#| The discrete energy after each of `periods` periods, relative to the first.
def energy_drift(n, periods) {
    h = 1.0 / (n + 1.0)
    per_period = round(2.0 / (C * NU * h))
    dt = 2.0 / (C * per_period)
    nu = C * dt / h
    x = linspace(h, 1.0 - h, n)
    old = sin(pi * x)
    u = old + 0.5 * nu * nu * second_difference(old, n)
    first = 0.0
    worst = 0.0
    for p to periods {
        for s to per_period {
            new = 2.0 * u - old + nu * nu * second_difference(u, n)
            old = u
            u = new
        }
        # energy at the half step: kinetic from (u - old)/dt, potential from the two levels
        v = (u - old) / dt
        e = 0.5 * sum(v * v) * h - 0.5 * C * C * sum(u * second_difference(old, n)) / h
        if p == 0.0 { first = e }
        worst = max(worst, abs(e - first) / first)
    }
    return worst
}

solvers.title: A shock and a rarefaction in inviscid Burgers' equation
solvers.equationHtml: ut​+(21​u2)x​=0
solvers.methodHtml: Godunov's method: the exact Riemann solution at every cell face
solvers.checksHtml: the shock speed, exact conservation, and the rarefaction fan u = x/t
notes: Take the viscosity away and smooth data stops being enough: characteristics cross, the derivative blows up in finite time, and the solution continues as a shock. A finite difference of a discontinuity means nothing, so the method has to be built on the integral form instead — what flows into a cell minus what flows out.
Godunov's answer: at each face the two neighboring cells pose a Riemann problem, which for Burgers has a closed-form solution; use its flux. For f=u2/2 that flux is max(f(max(uL​,0)), f(min(uR​,0))).

The same two states, in opposite orders, give opposite behavior. uL​>uR​ is a shock, moving at 21​(uL​+uR​). uL​<uR​ is a rarefaction: the jump opens into the fan u=x/t. A scheme that gets the first right by conserving, and the second right by not inventing an expansion shock, has earned the name entropy-satisfying.
solvers.sourceHtml: XMIN = -1.0 XMAX = 2.0 #| Godunov's flux at every face between a cell and its right neighbor. def godunov_flux(u) { ul = max(u, 0.0) ur = min(roll(u, -1.0), 0.0) return max(0.5 * ul * ul, 0.5 * ur * ur) } #| March n cells to t_end from a step (left state, right state) at x = 0. def march(n, t_end, left, right) { h = (XMAX - XMIN) / n u = zeros(n) for i to n { x = XMIN + (i + 0.5) * h u[i] = right if x < 0.0 { u[i] = left } } steps = round(t_end / (0.5 * h)) dt = t_end / steps hold = zeros(n) + 1.0 hold[0] = 0.0 hold[n - 1.0] = 0.0 for s to steps { f = godunov_flux(u) u = u - (dt / h) * (f - roll(f, 1.0)) * hold } return u } N = 300 H = (XMAX - XMIN) / N T_END = 1.2 shock = march(N, T_END, 1.0, 0.0) fan = march(N, T_END, 0.0, 1.0) # the shock: where is it, and was anything lost? mass = sum(shock) * H mass_exact = (0.0 - XMIN) + 0.5 * T_END position = XMIN + mass show mass show position # the fan: compare with u = x/t inside it fan_error = 0.0 X = zeros(N) FAN_EXACT = zeros(N) for i to N { X[i] = XMIN + (i + 0.5) * H e = 0.0 if X[i] > 0.0 { e = min(X[i] / T_END, 1.0) } FAN_EXACT[i] = e fan_error = fan_error + abs(fan[i] - e) * H } show fan_error figure("Two Riemann problems for Burgers' equation at t = 1.2", "x", "u") plot(X, shock, "$u_L = 1$, $u_R = 0$: a shock at $x = t/2$") plot(X, fan, "$u_L = 0$, $u_R = 1$: a rarefaction, computed") plot(X, FAN_EXACT, "the fan u = x/t, exact") test "conservation is exact: the mass is what flowed in, to rounding" { assert_near(mass, mass_exact, 1.0e-12) } test "so the shock sits at x = t/2, the Rankine-Hugoniot speed" { assert_near(position, 0.5 * T_END, 1.0e-12) } test "the shock is captured in at most three cells, with no overshoot" { worst = 0.0 smeared = 0.0 for i to N { worst = max(worst, shock[i] - 1.0) worst = max(worst, 0.0 - shock[i]) if shock[i] > 0.01 and shock[i] < 0.99 { smeared = smeared + 1.0 } } assert_lt(worst, 1.0e-12) assert_lt(smeared, 3.5) } test "the rarefaction opens into the fan u = x/t, not an expansion shock" { assert_lt(fan_error, 0.02) } # SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0 # SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 The Viv authors

solvers.title: The Euler equations of gas dynamics
solvers.equationHtml: ∂t​​ρρuE​​+∂x​​ρuρu2+p(E+p)u​​=0
solvers.methodHtml: finite volumes with the HLL approximate Riemann flux, first order; the exact solution is computed alongside
solvers.checksHtml: Sod's shock tube: the exact solution against the jump conditions, then the computed plateau, shock position, conservation and L1 convergence against it
notes: Mass, momentum and energy of a compressible gas, with p=(γ−1)(E−21​ρu2). Sod's problem is a membrane at x=21​ with dense, high-pressure gas on the left; at t=0 it bursts. Three waves come out: a rarefaction fan moving left, a contact discontinuity (density jumps, pressure and velocity do not) and a shock, both moving right.

Finite volumes store cell averages and move them by the fluxes through the cell walls, so whatever leaves one cell enters the next and the totals are conserved to rounding — which is what puts shocks at the right speed. The flux at a wall is a Riemann problem between the two neighbors. HLL does not solve it; it keeps only the fastest left- and right-going signal speeds sL​,sR​ and the one averaged state between them, which gives F=(sR+​FL​−sL−​FR​+sL−​sR+​(qR​−qL​))/(sR+​−sL−​), with s+=max(s,0), s−=min(s,0).

The exact solution needs one number, the pressure p∗ between the waves, which solves fL​(p)+fR​(p)+uR​−uL​=0; f is a shock branch or a rarefaction branch depending on the side of pK​ that p falls. It is monotone, so bisection finds it. Everything else follows in closed form. The jump conditions across the shock are tested directly from the conservation laws, so the exact solution is not taken on trust either.
A first-order scheme smears the contact over many cells (like t​) and the shock over a few, so in the L1 norm it converges at an order below one. That is measured, not hidden.
solvers.sourceHtml: G = 1.4 #: G ratio of specific heats, gamma RHO_L = 1.0 P_L = 1.0 RHO_R = 0.125 P_R = 0.1 T_END = 0.2 X_MEMBRANE = 0.5 NVAR = 3.0 #: NVAR conserved variables per cell: rho, rho u, E STAR_BISECTIONS = 80.0 #: STAR_BISECTIONS halvings of the bracket around the star pressure #| One side's term in the pressure equation: a shock if p is above that side's pressure, a rarefaction if below. def pressure_term(p, rho_k, p_k) { a_k = sqrt(G * p_k / rho_k) if p > p_k { return (p - p_k) * sqrt((2.0 / ((G + 1.0) * rho_k)) / (p + (G - 1.0) / (G + 1.0) * p_k)) } return 2.0 * a_k / (G - 1.0) * (pow(p / p_k, (G - 1.0) / (2.0 * G)) - 1.0) } #| The pressure between the waves, by bisection. Both gases start at rest. def star_pressure() { lo = 1.0e-9 hi = P_L for it to STAR_BISECTIONS { mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi) if pressure_term(mid, RHO_L, P_L) + pressure_term(mid, RHO_R, P_R) > 0.0 { hi = mid } else { lo = mid } } return 0.5 * (lo + hi) } P_STAR = star_pressure() U_STAR = 0.5 * (pressure_term(P_STAR, RHO_R, P_R) - pressure_term(P_STAR, RHO_L, P_L)) A_L = sqrt(G * P_L / RHO_L) A_R = sqrt(G * P_R / RHO_R) RHO_STAR_L = RHO_L * pow(P_STAR / P_L, 1.0 / G) # isentropic, through the fan GM = (G - 1.0) / (G + 1.0) RHO_STAR_R = RHO_R * (P_STAR / P_R + GM) / (GM * P_STAR / P_R + 1.0) # across the shock SHOCK_SPEED = A_R * sqrt((G + 1.0) / (2.0 * G) * P_STAR / P_R + (G - 1.0) / (2.0 * G)) TAIL_SPEED = U_STAR - A_L * pow(P_STAR / P_L, (G - 1.0) / (2.0 * G)) show P_STAR show U_STAR show RHO_STAR_L show RHO_STAR_R show SHOCK_SPEED #| The exact density at the points x, at time t: left state, fan, two plateaus, right state. def exact_density(x, t) { n = len(x) rho = zeros(n) for i to n { xi = (x[i] - X_MEMBRANE) / t if xi < -A_L { rho[i] = RHO_L } else if xi < TAIL_SPEED { rho[i] = RHO_L * pow(2.0 / (G + 1.0) - GM * xi / A_L, 2.0 / (G - 1.0)) } else if xi < U_STAR { rho[i] = RHO_STAR_L } else if xi < SHOCK_SPEED { rho[i] = RHO_STAR_R } else { rho[i] = RHO_R } } return rho } #| Pressure from the conserved variables, a 3 x m array of (rho, rho u, E). def pressure(q) { mom = slab(q, 1.0) return (G - 1.0) * (slab(q, 2.0) - 0.5 * mom * mom / slab(q, 0.0)) } #| The physical flux of each cell's state. def physical_flux(q) { rho = slab(q, 0.0) mom = slab(q, 1.0) p = pressure(q) u = mom / rho f = zeros(NVAR, len(rho)) setslab(f, 0.0, mom) setslab(f, 1.0, mom * u + p) setslab(f, 2.0, (slab(q, 2.0) + p) * u) return f } #| The HLL flux through every cell's RIGHT wall (column i: between cells i and i + 1). def hll_flux(q) { rho = slab(q, 0.0) u = slab(q, 1.0) / rho a = sqrt(G * pressure(q) / rho) s_left = min(min(u - a, roll(u - a, -1.0)), 0.0) s_right = max(max(u + a, roll(u + a, -1.0)), 0.0) f = physical_flux(q) f_next = roll(f, -1.0, 1.0) q_next = roll(q, -1.0, 1.0) out = zeros(NVAR, len(rho)) for k to NVAR { fl = slab(f, k) fr = slab(f_next, k) dq = slab(q_next, k) - slab(q, k) setslab(out, k, (s_right * fl - s_left * fr + s_left * s_right * dq) / (s_right - s_left)) } return out } #| Sod's initial state on n cells plus one ghost cell at each end. def initial_state(n) { dx = 1.0 / n q = zeros(NVAR, n + 2.0) for i to n + 2.0 { x = (i - 0.5) * dx if x < X_MEMBRANE { q[0, i] = RHO_L q[2, i] = P_L / (G - 1.0) } else { q[0, i] = RHO_R q[2, i] = P_R / (G - 1.0) } } return q } #| March n cells to T_END at a Courant number of 0.9. The ghost cells copy their neighbors. def solve_sod(n) { dx = 1.0 / n q = initial_state(n) t = 0.0 while t < T_END { rho = slab(q, 0.0) speed = max(abs(slab(q, 1.0) / rho) + sqrt(G * pressure(q) / rho)) dt = min(0.9 * dx / speed, T_END - t) f = hll_flux(q) q = q - (dt / dx) * (f - roll(f, 1.0, 1.0)) for k to NVAR { q[k, 0] = q[k, 1] q[k, n + 1.0] = q[k, n] } t = t + dt } return q } #| Cell centers, ghosts included. def centers(n) { dx = 1.0 / n return linspace(-0.5 * dx, 1.0 + 0.5 * dx, n + 2.0) } #| L1 error of the density over the interior cells. def density_error(n) { d = abs(slab(solve_sod(n), 0.0) - exact_density(centers(n), T_END)) return (sum(d) - d[0] - d[n + 1.0]) / n } N = 400 X = centers(N) Q = solve_sod(N) RHO = slab(Q, 0.0) VEL = slab(Q, 1.0) / RHO PRS = pressure(Q) # conservation: nothing has reached the walls, so interior mass and energy cannot have changed mass = (sum(RHO) - RHO[0] - RHO[N + 1.0]) / N energy = (sum(slab(Q, 2.0)) - Q[2, 0] - Q[2, N + 1.0]) / N mass_0 = 0.5 * (RHO_L + RHO_R) energy_0 = 0.5 * (P_L + P_R) / (G - 1.0) momentum = (sum(slab(Q, 1.0)) - Q[1, 0] - Q[1, N + 1.0]) / N show mass show energy show momentum # the plateau between contact and shock, sampled at its middle x_contact = X_MEMBRANE + U_STAR * T_END x_shock = X_MEMBRANE + SHOCK_SPEED * T_END i_mid = round(0.5 * (x_contact + x_shock) * N + 0.5) plateau_u = VEL[i_mid] plateau_p = PRS[i_mid] show plateau_u show plateau_p # the computed shock: where the density crosses halfway between the two states it separates found_shock = 0.0 for i to N { half = 0.5 * (RHO_STAR_R + RHO_R) if RHO[i] >= half and RHO[i + 1.0] < half { found_shock = X[i] + (X[i + 1.0] - X[i]) * (RHO[i] - half) / (RHO[i] - RHO[i + 1.0]) } } show x_shock show found_shock err_200 = density_error(200.0) err_400 = density_error(400.0) l1_order = log(err_200 / err_400) / log(2.0) show err_200 show err_400 show l1_order figure("Sod's shock tube at t = 0.2: fan, contact, shock", "x", "density") plot(X, exact_density(X, T_END), "exact") plot(X, RHO, "HLL, 400 cells") style("exact", "dash") test "the exact shock obeys the jump conditions: mass and momentum through it balance" { mass_in = RHO_R * (0.0 - solvers.title: Laplace's equation
solvers.equationHtml: ∇2u=0
solvers.methodHtml: successive over-relaxation, with the optimal relaxation factor for a square
solvers.checksHtml: a value symmetry fixes exactly; and that over-relaxation beats plain Gauss-Seidel by the factor theory predicts
notes: A square plate: one edge held at 1, the other three at 0. What is the temperature at the center?

Exactly 41​, and no series is needed to see it. Solve the problem four times, heating each edge in turn, and add the answers: the sum has every edge at 1, so it is 1 everywhere. By symmetry each of the four gives the same value at the center. The discrete equations have the same symmetry, so the numerical answer is 41​ too — to the solver's tolerance, not the grid's. It is the rare test with no discretization error in it.

Gauss-Seidel replaces each point by the average of its neighbors, sweep after sweep, and is slow: the error shrinks by a factor of about 1−π2h2 per sweep. SOR moves each point a factor ω past that average. With ω=2/(1+sinπh) the factor becomes about 1−2πh, and the number of sweeps drops from O(n2) to O(n).
solvers.source:
pi = 3.141592653589793
SWEEPS = zeros(1)       #: SWEEPS  how many sweeps the last solve took

#| Relax to convergence with relaxation factor omega; returns the grid.
def relax(n, omega, tol) {
    u = zeros(n + 2.0, n + 2.0)
    for j to n + 2.0 {
        u[0.0, j] = 1.0
    }
    change = 1.0
    sweeps = 0.0
    while change > tol and sweeps < 20000.0 {
        change = 0.0
        for i to n {
            for j to n {
                a = i + 1.0
                b = j + 1.0
                avg = 0.25 * (u[a - 1.0, b] + u[a + 1.0, b] + u[a, b - 1.0] + u[a, b + 1.0])
                step = omega * (avg - u[a, b])
                u[a, b] = u[a, b] + step
                change = max(change, abs(step))
            }
        }
        sweeps = sweeps + 1.0
    }
    SWEEPS[0] = sweeps
    return u
}

N = 23
H = 1.0 / (N + 1.0)
OMEGA = 2.0 / (1.0 + sin(pi * H))
u_sor = relax(N, OMEGA, 1.0e-12)
sor_sweeps = SWEEPS[0]
u_gs = relax(N, 1.0, 1.0e-12)
gs_sweeps = SWEEPS[0]
center = u_sor[(N + 1.0) / 2.0, (N + 1.0) / 2.0]
speedup = gs_sweeps / sor_sweeps
show OMEGA
show center
show sor_sweeps
show gs_sweeps
show speedup

# transposed, the first index of u_sor runs across and the second up, so the hot
# edge, u[0, j] = 1, is on the left
figure("A plate with one hot edge", "x", "y")
origin("lower")
plot2d(transpose(u_sor), "temperature")

test "the center of the plate is exactly 1/4, by symmetry" {
    assert_near(center, 0.25, 1.0e-10)
}
test "Gauss-Seidel reaches the same answer" {
    assert_near(u_gs[(N + 1.0) / 2.0, (N + 1.0) / 2.0], 0.25, 1.0e-9)
}
test "optimal over-relaxation needs an order of magnitude fewer sweeps" {
    assert_gt(speedup, 10.0)
    assert_lt(sor_sweeps, 5.0 * N)
}

solvers.title: Poisson's equation
solvers.equationHtml: −∇2u=f
solvers.methodHtml: five-point Laplacian, solved by conjugate gradients without ever forming the matrix
solvers.checksHtml: a manufactured solution; the measured order; and that conjugate gradients converges in far fewer steps than unknowns
notes: The equation of electrostatics, steady heat flow and pressure in an incompressible fluid. There is no time to march through: every unknown depends on every other, and the work is solving a large sparse linear system.

Pick the answer first — u=sin(πx)sin(2πy)+x(1−x)y(1−y), zero on the boundary of the unit square — and the right-hand side follows by differentiating: f=5π2sin(πx)sin(2πy)+2x(1−x)+2y(1−y). That is a manufactured solution, and it turns "is the solver right?" into a subtraction.

The polynomial term is there on purpose. A pure sine product is an eigenvector of the discrete Laplacian, and conjugate gradients solves an eigenvector problem in ONE step — which would make the iteration count below meaningless. The bubble x(1−x)y(1−y) has a piece of every mode.

The five-point Laplacian is symmetric positive definite, which is exactly what conjugate gradients wants. CG only ever needs the matrix applied to a vector, so the matrix is never built: the grid carries a ring of zeros around it, a neighbor is a roll, and a mask puts the boundary back to zero.
solvers.sourceHtml: pi = 3.141592653589793 #| Apply -h^2 Laplacian to a padded (n+2) x (n+2) grid; the boundary ring stays zero. def apply_laplacian(u, mask) { lap = 4.0 * u - roll(u, 1.0, 0.0) - roll(u, -1.0, 0.0) - roll(u, 1.0, 1.0) - roll(u, -1.0, 1.0) return lap * mask } #| 1 on interior points, 0 on the boundary ring. def interior_mask(n) { m = zeros(n + 2.0, n + 2.0) for i to n { for j to n { m[i + 1.0, j + 1.0] = 1.0 } } return m } #| The manufactured solution sampled on the padded grid. def exact_solution(n) { h = 1.0 / (n + 1.0) x = reshape(arange(n + 2.0) * h, -1, 1) # a column: x runs down the rows y = arange(n + 2.0) * h # a row: y runs across return sin(pi * x) * sin(2.0 * pi * y) + x * (1.0 - x) * y * (1.0 - y) } #| Its right-hand side, f = -Laplacian(u), worked out by hand. def right_hand_side(n) { h = 1.0 / (n + 1.0) x = reshape(arange(n + 2.0) * h, -1, 1) y = arange(n + 2.0) * h return 5.0 * pi * pi * sin(pi * x) * sin(2.0 * pi * y) + 2.0 * x * (1.0 - x) + 2.0 * y * (1.0 - y) } ITERS = zeros(1) #: ITERS how many CG steps the last solve took (a one-element out-parameter) #| Solve -Laplacian u = f on an n x n interior by conjugate gradients. def solve_poisson(n) { h = 1.0 / (n + 1.0) mask = interior_mask(n) b = (h * h) * right_hand_side(n) * mask u = zeros(n + 2.0, n + 2.0) r = b p = r rr = sum(r * r) target = 1.0e-20 * rr k = 0.0 while rr > target and k < 2000.0 { ap = apply_laplacian(p, mask) alpha = rr / sum(p * ap) u = u + alpha * p r = r - alpha * ap rr_new = sum(r * r) p = r + (rr_new / rr) * p rr = rr_new k = k + 1.0 } ITERS[0] = k return u } #| L2 error of the solve on an n x n grid. def poisson_error(n) { h = 1.0 / (n + 1.0) d = solve_poisson(n) - exact_solution(n) return sqrt(sum(d * d)) * h } e1 = poisson_error(16.0) e2 = poisson_error(33.0) iters = ITERS[0] order = log(e1 / e2) / log(2.0) show e1 show e2 show order show iters # u[i, j] is the solution at x = i h, y = j h: transposed, x runs across and y up figure("The solution of Poisson's equation", "x", "y") origin("lower") plot2d(transpose(solve_poisson(40.0)), "u") test "the solve matches the manufactured solution" { assert_lt(e2, 2.0e-3) } test "the five-point Laplacian is second order" { assert_near(order, 2.0, 0.1) } test "conjugate gradients needs far fewer steps than there are unknowns (33 x 33 = 1089)" { assert_lt(iters, 120.0) } # SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0 # SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 The Viv authors

solvers.title: The modes of a drum, a Helmholtz eigenproblem
solvers.equationHtml: −∇2u=λu
solvers.methodHtml: the five-point Laplacian as a dense symmetric matrix, diagonalized by eig_sym
solvers.checksHtml: the discrete eigenvalues against their closed form (to rounding), the continuum ones to second order, and the degeneracy a square must have
notes: Separate variables in the wave equation and what is left is an eigenproblem: the shapes a membrane can vibrate in, and the frequencies that go with them. For a unit square fixed at its edge the answer is known, λmn​=π2(m2+n2) with u=sin(mπx)sin(nπy).

The five-point Laplacian has the same eigenvectors, sampled on the grid, and eigenvalues known in closed form as well: λmnh​=h24​(sin22mπh​+sin22nπh​). So there are two checks of different kinds. Against the discrete formula the eigensolver must agree to rounding — that tests eig_sym. Against π2(m2+n2) it agrees only to O(h2) — that tests the discretization.
A square also forces a degeneracy: (m,n)=(1,2) and (2,1) have the same frequency, so the second and third eigenvalues must coincide. Any asymmetry in the assembled matrix would split them.

solvers.title: The time-dependent Schrödinger equation
solvers.equationHtml: iψt​=−21​ψxx​+V(x)ψ
solvers.methodHtml: split-step Fourier (Strang splitting): the kinetic step is exact in momentum space
solvers.checksHtml: a free packet's spreading, a coherent state's oscillation, norm conservation, and the measured order of the splitting
notes: Two operators, each trivial in its own basis. The potential multiplies ψ(x) by a phase; the kinetic energy multiplies ψ^​(k) by a phase. Neither can be applied exactly to the other's representation — but an FFT moves between them, so alternate: half a potential step, a full kinetic step, half a potential step. That is Strang splitting. Every factor is a pure phase, so the norm is conserved to rounding whatever the time step, and the error is O(Δt2), from the two operators failing to commute.
Free particle. With V=0 there is nothing to split and one step of any length is exact. A Gaussian packet moves at its group velocity k0​ and spreads as σ(t)=σ0​1+(t/2σ02​)2​.
Harmonic oscillator. In V=21​x2 the ground state displaced to x0​ is a coherent state: it keeps its shape and its center follows the classical orbit, ⟨x⟩=x0​cost.

Where you look for the splitting error matters. For this potential Strang splitting solves, exactly, an oscillator whose frequency is off by O(Δt2) — so the computed center is x0​cos(t+δ) with a phase error δ∝Δt2. After a FULL period that is x0​(1−δ2/2): the error is quadratic in δ and the scheme looks fourth order. At a QUARTER period, where the orbit crosses the origin, it is −x0​δ, and the true order shows. Both are measured below.

solvers.title: The Korteweg-de Vries equation
solvers.equationHtml: ut​+6uux​+uxxx​=0
solvers.methodHtml: Fourier pseudo-spectral in space; Strang splitting in time, with the dispersive step exact
solvers.checksHtml: a soliton against its exact solution: shape, speed, conserved mass, and the measured order
notes: Shallow-water waves, and the equation solitons were discovered in. Nonlinearity steepens a hump; third-order dispersion spreads it; and for exactly one family of shapes the two cancel: u=2c​sech2(2c​​(x−ct−x0​)). Taller solitons are narrower and faster — the speed c is twice the height.

uxxx​ is the hard part for finite differences: an explicit scheme needs Δt∼Δx3. In Fourier space it is trivial — each mode just turns, u^k​→u^k​eik3Δt, exactly, for any Δt. So split: half a dispersive step, a full step of the nonlinear part ut​=−3(u2)x​ (spectral derivative, fourth-order Runge-Kutta), half a dispersive step.
The Nyquist mode is zeroed in the derivative. On an even grid it has no well-defined sign, and leaving it in makes the derivative of a real field complex.
solvers.source:
pi = 3.141592653589793
N = 256
L = 40.0
DX = L / N
X = linspace(-0.5 * L, 0.5 * L - DX, N)
K = zeros(N)
for j to N {
    K[j] = 2.0 * pi * j / L
    if j >= N / 2.0 { K[j] = 2.0 * pi * (j - N) / L }
}
K[N / 2.0] = 0.0
ZERO = zeros(N)
IK = complex(ZERO, K)

C = 2.0
X0 = -6.0

#| The soliton of speed C at time t.
def soliton(t) {
    s = 1.0 / cosh(0.5 * sqrt(C) * (X - C * t - X0))
    return 0.5 * C * s * s
}

#| The nonlinear rate, -3 d/dx (u^2), with the derivative taken in Fourier space.
def nonlinear_rate(u) {
    d = complex(u * u, ZERO)
    fft(d)
    d = d * IK
    ifft(d)
    return -3.0 * re(d)
}

#| The dispersive step, exact: every mode turns by exp(i k^3 dt).
def disperse(u, dt) {
    v = complex(u, ZERO)
    fft(v)
    theta = K * K * K * dt
    v = v * complex(cos(theta), sin(theta))
    ifft(v)
    return re(v)
}

#| March the soliton to t_end in `steps` Strang steps.
def march(t_end, steps) {
    dt = t_end / steps
    u = soliton(0.0)
    for s to steps {
        u = disperse(u, 0.5 * dt)
        k1 = nonlinear_rate(u)
        k2 = nonlinear_rate(u + 0.5 * dt * k1)
        k3 = nonlinear_rate(u + 0.5 * dt * k2)
        k4 = nonlinear_rate(u + dt * k3)
        u = u + (dt / 6.0) * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4)
        u = disperse(u, 0.5 * dt)
    }
    return u
}

#| Where the hump is: its center of mass. A sum over a periodic grid is spectrally accurate
#| for a pulse that has decayed before the edges, so this locates it far below the spacing
#| (a parabola through the top three points is off by 2e-4 here, and no time step fixes that).
def center(u) {
    return sum(X * u) / sum(u)
}

T_END = 2.0
u = march(T_END, 1600.0)
d = u - soliton(T_END)
shape_error = sqrt(sum(d * d) * DX)
mass_drift = abs(sum(u) - sum(soliton(0.0))) * DX
speed = (center(u) - X0) / T_END
d1 = march(T_END, 200.0) - soliton(T_END)
d2 = march(T_END, 400.0) - soliton(T_END)
order = log(sqrt(sum(d1 * d1)) / sqrt(sum(d2 * d2))) / log(2.0)
show shape_error
show mass_drift
show speed
show order

figure("A soliton of speed 2: it moves, and nothing else happens", "x", "u")
plot(X, soliton(0.0), "t = 0")
plot(X, u, "t = 2, computed")
plot(X, soliton(T_END), "t = 2, exact")
style("t = 2, exact", "dash")

test "the soliton keeps its shape" {
    assert_lt(shape_error, 1.0e-5)
}
test "it moves at c, twice its height" {
    assert_near(speed, C, 1.0e-4)
}
test "mass is conserved to rounding: a spectral derivative has exactly zero mean" {
    assert_lt(mass_drift, 1.0e-12)
}
test "the splitting is second order" {
    assert_near(order, 2.0, 0.1)
}


# Two solitons: the taller one starts behind, catches the shorter, and passes through it.
# Hirota's exact two-soliton solution is u = 2 (log tau)_xx with
# tau = 1 + e^eta1 + e^eta2 + A e^(eta1 + eta2), eta_i = k_i (x - x_i) - k_i^3 t and
# A = ((k1 - k2) / (k1 + k2))^2; soliton i has speed k_i^2 and height k_i^2 / 2.
# After the collision each is where it would be, shifted: the taller ahead, the shorter behind.
K1 = 1.6
K2 = 1.0
X1 = -13.0
X2 = -5.0
T2_END = 8.0
T2_STEPS = 1600
# a row of the waterfall every this many steps, every other grid point
T2_EVERY = 40
X_STRIDE = 2

#| Hirota's exact two-soliton solution on the grid X at time t.
#@ 5cc5e18a
def two_solitons(t) {
    A = (K1 - K2) * (K1 - K2) / ((K1 + K2) * (K1 + K2))
    e1 = exp(K1 * (X - X1) - K1 * K1 * K1 * t)
    e2 = exp(K2 * (X - X2) - K2 * K2 * K2 * t)
    e12 = A * e1 * e2
    tau = 1.0 + e1 + e2 + e12
    d1 = K1 * e1 + K2 * e2 + (K1 + K2) * e12
    d2 = K1 * K1 * e1 + K2 * K2 * e2 + (K1 + K2) * (K1 + K2) * e12
    return 2.0 * (d2 * tau - d1 * d1) / (tau * tau)
}

n_rows = T2_STEPS / T2_EVERY + 1
n_cols = N / X_STRIDE
waterfall = zeros(n_rows, n_cols)
w = two_solitons(0.0)
dt2 = T2_END / T2_STEPS
for s to T2_STEPS + 1 {
    if mod(s, T2_EVERY) == 0 {
        for c to n_cols {
            waterfall[s / T2_EVERY, c] = round(1.0e4 * w[c * X_STRIDE]) / 1.0e4
        }
    }
    if s < T2_STEPS {
        w = disperse(w, 0.5 * dt2)
        q1 = nonlinear_rate(w)
        q2 = nonlinear_rate(w + 0.5 * dt2 * q1)
        q3 = nonlinear_rate(w + 0.5 * dt2 * q2)
        q4 = nonlinear_rate(w + dt2 * q3)
        w = w + (dt2 / 6.0) * (q1 + 2.0 * q2 + 2.0 * q3 + q4)
        w = disperse(w, 0.5 * dt2)
    }
}
dw = w - two_solitons(T2_END)
collision_error = max(abs(dw))
show collision_error

figure("Two solitons collide and pass through each other", "x", "t", -0.5 * L, 0.5 * L - DX, 0.0, T2_END)
origin("lower")
plot2d(waterfall, "u")

test "after the collision the two solitons are Hirota's exact solution, phase shifts included" {
    # the splitting's second-order error at dt = 0.005 is 3.2e-4; at dt = 0.0025 it is 7.8e-5
    assert_lt(collision_error, 5.0e-4)
}

solvers.title: The nonlinear Schrödinger equation
solvers.equationHtml: iψt​+21​ψxx​+∣ψ∣2ψ=0
solvers.methodHtml: split-step Fourier: the nonlinear step is ALSO exact, because it conserves the modulus
solvers.checksHtml: the bright soliton sech(x) exp(it/2): its shape, its phase, the conserved norm, and the measured order
notes: Light in a fiber, a Bose-Einstein condensate, deep-water wave envelopes. Dispersion spreads a pulse; the focusing nonlinearity squeezes it. When they balance the pulse is a soliton, and the simplest is ψ=sech(x)eit/2: a shape that does not change at all, with a phase that turns at a steady rate.

Split-step works even better here than for the linear equation. The nonlinear part alone, iψt​=−∣ψ∣2ψ, leaves ∣ψ∣ unchanged — so its solution is exactly ψ→ψei∣ψ∣2Δt, no time-stepping error. Both halves are exact; the only error is the splitting itself.
solvers.sourceHtml: pi = 3.141592653589793 N = 256 L = 40.0 DX = L / N X = linspace(-0.5 * L, 0.5 * L - DX, N) K = zeros(N) for j to N { K[j] = 2.0 * pi * j / L if j >= N / 2.0 { K[j] = 2.0 * pi * (j - N) / L } } SECH = 1.0 / cosh(X) #| exp(+i theta) for a real array theta. def phase(theta) { return complex(cos(theta), sin(theta)) } #| Evolve the soliton to time t_end in `steps` Strang steps. def evolve(t_end, steps) { dt = t_end / steps dispersion = phase(-0.5 * K * K * dt) psi = complex(SECH, zeros(N)) for s to steps { psi = psi * phase(0.5 * dt * abs(psi) * abs(psi)) fft(psi) psi = psi * dispersion ifft(psi) psi = psi * phase(0.5 * dt * abs(psi) * abs(psi)) } return psi } #| The phase of psi at x = 0, in radians. def center_phase(psi) { z = psi[N / 2.0] return atan2(im(z), re(z)) } T_END = 2.0 psi = evolve(T_END, 400.0) shape = abs(psi) - SECH shape_error = sqrt(sum(shape * shape) * DX) norm = sum(abs(psi) * abs(psi)) * DX phase_now = center_phase(psi) p1 = abs(center_phase(evolve(T_END, 100.0)) - 0.5 * T_END) p2 = abs(center_phase(evolve(T_END, 200.0)) - 0.5 * T_END) order = log(p1 / p2) / log(2.0) show shape_error show norm show phase_now show order figure("A bright soliton: the modulus does not move", "x", "$|\\psi|$") plot(X, SECH, "t = 0") plot(X, abs(psi), "t = 2") test "the soliton keeps its shape: |psi| is still sech(x)" { assert_lt(shape_error, 1.0e-5) } test "its phase turns at rate 1/2: arg psi(0, t) = t/2" { assert_near(phase_now, 0.5 * T_END, 1.0e-4) } test "the norm, 2 for sech(x), is conserved to rounding" { assert_near(norm, 2.0, 1.0e-10) } test "the splitting is second order" { assert_near(order, 2.0, 0.1) } # SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0 # SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 The Viv authors

solvers.title: Burgers' equation, viscous
solvers.equationHtml: ut​+uux​=νuxx​
solvers.methodHtml: conservative centered differences in space, fourth-order Runge-Kutta in time
solvers.checksHtml: the exact travelling-wave solution, its speed, and the measured order
notes: The smallest equation with both of a fluid's habits in it: uux​ steepens a wave, and νuxx​ smooths it. Where they balance the wave stops changing shape and simply travels: u=c−atanh(2νa(x−ct−x0​)​), a smoothed step from c+a down to c−a, of width about 4ν/a, moving at the mean of the two states.
That speed is the Rankine-Hugoniot condition, and it survives the limit ν→0: it is the speed of the shock the inviscid equation forms.

The nonlinear term is differenced in conservation form, ∂x​(u2/2), not as uux​. The two agree for smooth u, but only the first makes the scheme conserve ∫udx, and a scheme that does not conserve gets the wave speed wrong.
solvers.source:
NU = 0.02
UL = 1.0
UR = 0.0
CSPEED = 0.5 * (UL + UR)
AMP = 0.5 * (UL - UR)
X0 = 0.7
XMAX = 3.0

#| The exact travelling wave at time t.
def exact_wave(x, t) {
    return CSPEED - AMP * tanh(AMP * (x - CSPEED * t - X0) / (2.0 * NU))
}

#| du/dt on the grid. The two end points are held (their rate is zeroed by `hold`).
def rate(u, h, hold) {
    right = roll(u, -1.0)
    left = roll(u, 1.0)
    flux = 0.5 * (0.5 * right * right - 0.5 * left * left) / h
    diffusion = NU * (right - 2.0 * u + left) / (h * h)
    return (diffusion - flux) * hold
}

#| March to t_end with RK4 on n points; returns the solution.
def march(n, t_end) {
    h = XMAX / (n - 1.0)
    x = linspace(0.0, XMAX, n)
    u = exact_wave(x, 0.0)
    hold = zeros(n) + 1.0
    hold[0] = 0.0
    hold[n - 1.0] = 0.0
    steps = round(t_end / (0.2 * h * h / NU))
    dt = t_end / steps
    for s to steps {
        k1 = rate(u, h, hold)
        k2 = rate(u + 0.5 * dt * k1, h, hold)
        k3 = rate(u + 0.5 * dt * k2, h, hold)
        k4 = rate(u + dt * k3, h, hold)
        u = u + (dt / 6.0) * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4)
    }
    return u
}

#| L2 error against the exact wave.
def wave_error(n, t_end) {
    h = XMAX / (n - 1.0)
    x = linspace(0.0, XMAX, n)
    d = march(n, t_end) - exact_wave(x, t_end)
    return sqrt(sum(d * d) * h)
}

#| Where u crosses the mid-value, by linear interpolation: the front's position.
def front_position(u, n) {
    h = XMAX / (n - 1.0)
    pos = 0.0
    for i to n - 1.0 {
        if u[i] >= CSPEED and u[i + 1.0] < CSPEED {
            pos = (i + (u[i] - CSPEED) / (u[i] - u[i + 1.0])) * h
        }
    }
    return pos
}

T_END = 2.0
e1 = wave_error(151.0, T_END)
e2 = wave_error(301.0, T_END)
order = log(e1 / e2) / log(2.0)
N = 301
U = march(N, T_END)
speed = (front_position(U, N) - X0) / T_END
show e1
show e2
show order
show speed

X = linspace(0.0, XMAX, N)
figure("A viscous shock, travelling at the mean of its two states", "x", "u")
plot(X, exact_wave(X, 0.0), "t = 0")
plot(X, U, "t = 2, computed")
plot(X, exact_wave(X, T_END), "t = 2, exact")
style("t = 2, exact", "dash")

test "the computed wave matches the exact tanh profile" {
    assert_lt(e2, 1.0e-3)
}
test "the front moves at (u_left + u_right) / 2, the Rankine-Hugoniot speed" {
    assert_near(speed, CSPEED, 1.0e-3)
}
test "the scheme is second order in space" {
    assert_near(order, 2.0, 0.15)
}

solvers.title: The Fisher-KPP equation
solvers.equationHtml: ut​=uxx​+u(1−u)
solvers.methodHtml: Strang splitting: the logistic reaction solved exactly, diffusion by Crank-Nicolson
solvers.checksHtml: the front speed against the KPP value 2, approached from below with Bramson's logarithmic correction
notes: A population that grows logistically and spreads by diffusion: a gene through a species, a flame, an invading plant. Behind the front u=1, ahead of it u=0, and the front advances at a constant speed.

Which speed is the subtle part. Travelling waves exist for every c≥2; what is selected, from any initial condition that starts out compact, is the slowest, c∗=2rD​=2 — set entirely by the linearized growth at the front's leading edge, where u is tiny.

And it is approached slowly. Bramson showed the front sits at X(t)=2t−23​lnt+O(1), so the speed measured between two times is 2−23​ln(t2​/t1​)/(t2​−t1​), below 2 by an amount that dies only like 1/t. Measure between t=20 and 40 and the prediction is 1.948, not 2.
The reaction alone is the logistic equation, which has a closed form, so that half of the split has no time-stepping error at all.
